Family Health

Swollen labia: causes, treatment and when to seek help

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The labia are the outer and inner folds of the vulva, around the vaginal opening; the vagina is the internal canal. Their size, shape and symmetry vary naturally. A new change in swelling, especially with pain, itching, discharge or a lump, needs attention to its cause rather than treatment based on appearance alone.

Normal variation and symptoms to notice

One labium may normally be larger than the other. Temporary changes can also occur with arousal or pregnancy-related blood flow. These do not explain every new swelling. Notice whether the change affects one side or both, appeared suddenly, follows a product or activity, or keeps returning.

Associated symptoms can include itching, burning, soreness, changed vaginal discharge or smell, a lump, pain when walking or sitting, painful sex or stinging when urine touches irritated skin. None identifies a particular infection by itself. A persistent sore, bleeding skin or a changing patch or lump also deserves examination.

Yeast infection is one possible cause

Candida overgrowth can cause vulval redness, itching, soreness, swelling and sometimes thick discharge. Recent antibiotics, pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes or reduced immunity can increase the likelihood, but many people have no obvious trigger. These symptoms overlap with other conditions, so having had thrush before does not make self-diagnosis reliable.

Confirmed yeast infection is treated with an appropriate antifungal; severe, recurrent or persistent symptoms may need testing and a different plan. In pregnancy, current CDC guidance recommends a topical azole for seven days and advises against oral fluconazole. Check treatment with your maternity clinician or pharmacist. An asymptomatic partner does not routinely need treatment for uncomplicated thrush; a partner with symptoms should be assessed.

Bacterial vaginosis is not a fungal infection

Bacterial vaginosis, or BV, is a change in the balance of vaginal bacteria, not yeast overgrowth. It may cause thin discharge and a fishy smell, or no symptoms. Marked swelling or pain should not automatically be labelled BV; another cause or more than one condition may be present. BV is not proof of poor hygiene or infidelity.

Symptomatic BV is treated with clinician-selected antibiotics, not antifungal cream. Recurrence is common. Partner advice has changed with newer evidence: 2025–2026 guidance supports discussing concurrent treatment of ongoing partners, especially with recurrent symptomatic BV, while evidence and recommendations differ by situation. Ask the sexual-health clinician about the appropriate plan for you and your partners; do not share medicines or assume partners never need care.

Trichomoniasis and other sexually transmitted infections

Trichomoniasis is caused by a parasite transmitted through sexual contact. It can cause vulval irritation, altered discharge, odour or painful urination, but many people have few or no symptoms. Testing distinguishes it from yeast or BV; colour or smell cannot do that. Other infections, including genital herpes, can also cause vulval symptoms and need their own assessment.

Trichomoniasis requires an effective prescribed medicine and treatment of current sexual partners, even when they have no symptoms. Avoid sex until everyone has completed treatment and symptoms have resolved. Testing for other STIs is advised; women treated for trichomoniasis are generally retested at about three months because reinfection is common. Ask for individual pregnancy and follow-up advice rather than using leftover tablets or a vaginal antifungal.

Contact irritation, allergy and friction

Perfumed soaps, detergents, wipes, deodorants, some pads, latex, spermicides or a lubricant can irritate sensitive vulval skin or trigger an allergy. A product previously tolerated can still become a problem. Stop a suspected irritant and tell the clinician what you have used. Dermatitis and other skin conditions may need specific treatment; do not start steroid cream for unexplained swelling without advice.

Sexual activity with insufficient lubrication can cause friction and soreness. Stop if it hurts; consent and comfort take priority. When symptoms have settled and no treatment restriction applies, a suitable unperfumed lubricant may reduce friction. Check compatibility with condoms and any medicine, since some oils and creams weaken latex. If latex or spermicide seems responsible, ask about suitable alternatives that retain the protection you need.

A one-sided lump may be a Bartholin cyst or abscess

Bartholin glands lie near either side of the vaginal opening. A blocked duct can form a small, painless cyst; infection may produce a very painful abscess, swelling, pus or fever. A growing painful lump, hot or red swelling, or feeling unwell needs urgent same-day assessment. Do not squeeze, puncture or drain it yourself.

Have any new vulval lump examined. A new Bartholin-area mass at age 40 or older, or after menopause, needs particular attention; the clinician may recommend a biopsy to rule out uncommon malignancy. A small confirmed cyst may need observation and gentle warm-water comfort measures. A symptomatic cyst or abscess may require a drainage procedure, a catheter or another treatment, sometimes with antibiotics; removal of the gland is not automatic.

How the cause is assessed and treated

A clinician asks about onset, pain, discharge, products, medicines, previous episodes, medical conditions, sexual exposure and possible pregnancy, then examines with your consent. You can request a chaperone and ask to pause. Vaginal or skin samples, urine tests or STI tests may be selected according to the findings; not everyone needs every test.

A biopsy is a targeted investigation when a lesion looks concerning, a diagnosis remains unclear or symptoms fail to respond; it is not the routine test for every infection. Treatment follows the cause: antifungal for yeast, appropriate antibiotics for BV or trichomoniasis, removal of irritants and selected prescribed skin treatment, or cyst care. Reassessment matters if symptoms persist, worsen or recur rather than repeatedly treating presumed thrush.

Gentle comfort measures and remedies to avoid

Gently rinse the external vulva with lukewarm water and pat dry; avoid scrubbing, repeated washing, vaginal douching and scented products. Comfortable loose clothing and breathable underwear may reduce rubbing. A cool pack wrapped in a soft cloth can briefly soothe external irritation; do not place ice directly on skin or insert a pack into the vagina. For a diagnosed uncomplicated cyst, warm rather than hot water may help comfort, without delaying care for an abscess.

Pain relief should suit your health, pregnancy status and other medicines; ask a pharmacist or clinician if unsure. Yogurt and probiotic products are not proven substitutes for treatment of yeast or BV. Do not insert garlic, thyme preparations, tea tree oil, coconut oil or oregano oil, or assume a natural product is safe: they can irritate or cause allergy and do not reliably treat the cause. Avoid multiple over-the-counter creams that may worsen symptoms or obscure the diagnosis.

Recovery, follow-up and urgent symptoms

Many causes are treatable, but recovery depends on the diagnosis and swelling can recur. Arrange assessment for a new lump, persistent or recurrent swelling, unusual discharge or smell, sores, skin changes or pain. In pregnancy, contact your maternity clinician about new concerning genital symptoms before self-treatment. Keep the recommended follow-up and ask what to do if the first treatment does not help.

Seek urgent same-day care for a rapidly enlarging painful lump, fever, spreading redness, pus, or pelvic pain with unusual discharge or possible pregnancy. Seek immediate emergency care for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, fainting or collapse, heavy bleeding, confusion, breathing difficulty or acute inability to urinate. Swelling with throat or tongue symptoms or breathing difficulty may be a serious allergic reaction. Do not wait for a home remedy or an app entry to confirm the cause.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record the onset, affected side, associated symptoms, products and treatments used, and possible pregnancy for the appointment.

Ask which diagnosis and tests fit, what treatment is appropriate, and whether partners or follow-up testing need attention.

Know the difference between same-day assessment for a possible abscess and immediate care for severe systemic, urinary or allergic symptoms.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record symptoms, possible triggers, treatment instructions and questions for a clinician. It cannot diagnose swelling from a description or image, identify an infection, assess a lump or choose medicines or partner treatment. Seek care according to symptoms and follow clinical advice regardless of what the app records.

When to seek help

A painful rapidly growing lump, fever, pus, spreading redness or pelvic pain with unusual discharge or possible pregnancy needs urgent same-day assessment. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, collapse, heavy bleeding, confusion, breathing difficulty or acute inability to urinate needs immediate emergency care. Do not drain a lump or insert unproven remedies; pregnancy requires treatment-specific advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Labial size varies normally, but new swelling with symptoms needs its cause assessed.
  • Yeast, bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis are different conditions with different treatment and partner advice.
  • Avoid irritants, painful friction, douching and unproven inserted remedies; comfort measures do not replace diagnosis.
  • A painful growing lump or fever needs same-day care; severe pain, collapse, breathing problems or inability to urinate needs immediate help.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms can accompany swollen labia?

Itching, burning, soreness, altered discharge or smell, a lump and pain when walking, sitting, urinating or having sex may occur. No single symptom proves a particular infection. Persistent sores, bleeding skin or changing patches also need examination.

What can cause the swelling?

Possible causes include yeast infection, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, contact irritation or allergy, a Bartholin cyst or abscess, and friction. BV involves bacterial imbalance, not fungus. Other skin disorders or infections can look similar.

Can allergy cause swollen labia?

Yes. Latex, spermicides, scented products or other contact substances can cause irritation or allergy. Stop the suspected trigger and seek assessment if symptoms persist. Throat or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty or collapse needs immediate emergency care.

How is the cause diagnosed?

History and examination guide selected swabs, urine or STI tests. Biopsy is considered for particular concerning, unclear or persistent lesions rather than every case. Tell the clinician about products, medicines, sexual exposure and possible pregnancy.

Is swelling on one side always a Bartholin cyst?

No. A cyst is one possibility, but any new lump should be examined. A rapidly growing painful lump, pus or fever needs same-day care. A new Bartholin-area mass at age 40 or older or after menopause may need biopsy. Do not drain it yourself.

Can I use a yeast treatment during pregnancy?

Ask your maternity clinician or pharmacist to confirm the cause and treatment. For pregnancy-related yeast infection, CDC recommends a topical azole for seven days and advises against oral fluconazole. Swelling alone does not confirm thrush.

Does my partner need treatment?

For trichomoniasis, current sexual partners need treatment and sex should wait until treatment is completed and symptoms have resolved. Uncomplicated thrush does not routinely require treatment of an asymptomatic partner. Newer BV guidance supports discussing concurrent care for ongoing partners, especially with recurrent symptoms; a clinician should choose the plan.

Will yogurt, herbs or a cold pack cure it?

A wrapped cool pack may soothe external irritation, but does not treat the underlying cause. Yogurt, probiotics and inserted herbal or essential-oil products are not reliable cures and may irritate. Persistent, worsening or urgent symptoms need clinical care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
